question.problem:
The position $y(t),$ measured in meters, of a particle oscillating with forced harmonic motion with light damping is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}+2y=10{e}^{t},
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the particle is initially at the origin with velocity $4\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}$, find the particle's position after $\frac{\pi }{3}$ seconds.
question.worked_solution:
The general solution to the equation of forced harmonic motion with light damping is the sum of the complementary function and a particular solution.

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}+2y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +2 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2}+1 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda +1 & =\pm \text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-1\pm \text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{y}_{c}={e}^{-t}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡t+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡t).
$$

where $P$ and $Q$ are arbitrary constants of integration.

We now need to find the particular integral ${y}_{p}(t).$

The external force is an exponential force. The constant factor in the exponent is $1,$ which is not a root of the auxiliary equation. Therefore, we assume a particular exponential solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{t},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant to be determined. 

Substituting ${y}_{p}$ into the differential equation and equating coefficients gives $\alpha =2.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=2{e}^{t},
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y={e}^{-t}(P\operatorname{cos}⁡t+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2{e}^{t}.
$$

Since the particle is initially at the origin with velocity $4\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}$, the initial conditions are $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=4.$

Solving with these conditions for $P$ and $Q$ gives

$$
P=-2,\,Q=0.
$$

So our solution is

$$
y(t)=-2{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2{e}^{t}.
$$

To find the position of the particle after $\frac{\pi }{3}$ seconds, we substitute into the equation $t=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =-2{e}^{-\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})+2{e}^{\pi /3} \\  & =(-{e}^{-\pi /3}+2{e}^{\pi /3})\text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$
